lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
- Cut the monthly revenue report from 3 days of spreadsheet work to 2 hours by moving it to scheduled SQL queries and a shared dashboard.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.

- Joining 40 source tables, deduplicating customer records across two loyalty systems and rebuilding the attribution logic in dbt-style SQL models, raised the share of orders tied to a campaign from 58% to 81%.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Trained 20 merchandisers to answer their own questions with the self-serve dashboards, halving ad hoc data requests.
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Apr 2021 - Jul 2022
- Ran the checkout A/B test until significance by checking the p-value every day and stopping on the first day it fell below 0.05.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; the findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Wrote the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Leveraged data-driven insights and advanced analytics to unlock actionable value for urban mobility stakeholders.
- Cut empty-station hours from 300 to 200 a week, a 50% reduction, in a replay of last summer's rebalancing.
- Raised forecast hit rate by 15% across 120 stations, from 60% to 75%, by adding weather and event features.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- 9,000 handwritten visit logs were cleaned into a single table and repeat visitors were matched, so the pantry had its first count of unique households.
- Wrote a one-page guide the pantry coordinator used to update the visit table each month after the project ended.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: The file includes personal details conventionally left off a résumé.
items.because: Date of birth and nationality add personal information without strengthening the candidate’s qualifications.

items.says: Education appears before the candidate’s multi-year experience.
items.because: A reader should see the relevant work history before the degree.

items.says: There is a 10-month gap between graduation and the first listed role.
The join described cannot identify customers with no orders.
items.because: A left join from orders preserves orders, not customers without orders; a null customer name could indicate an unmatched order.

items.says: The finding does not say what action or decision it informed.
items.because: Naming the decision would show why identifying these customers mattered.

items.says: The finding gives neither the size of the group nor the period measured.
items.because: A count or share would show the scale, and a period would clarify what the measure covers.

items.says: The explanation of the join obscures the useful finding.
The 58% to 81% result is buried after a long method-led opening.
items.because: A scanning reader encounters several method details before learning what improved.

items.says: The review description does not identify the customer analysis behind the funded recommendations.
The A/B test uses repeated unadjusted significance testing, so stopping at the first p-value below 0.05 does not establish significance at that threshold.
items.because: Repeated checking and stopping at the first crossing inflates the false-positive rate above 5%.

items.says: The test line does not say what changed as a result.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the test improved checkout performance or informed a decision.

items.says: The threshold is given without the measured effect.
items.because: A p-value threshold does not show how large or useful the observed difference was.

items.says: The strongest result is not the opening line of the entry.
items.because: Putting the staffing change and hold-time reduction first would give a stronger first impression.

items.says: The call-center analysis does not say how it identified the evening peak.
Unrelated duties obscure the automation and its saving.
items.because: The 10-hour saving follows other responsibilities, making it harder to see that automating the extract produced it.

items.says: The Pinecrest entry’s workstreams read as separate rather than connected.
The project description uses generic language instead of naming the work or its outcome.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what changed or how its value was measured.

items.says: The change from 300 to 200 hours is a 33.3% reduction, not a 50% reduction.
items.because: The decrease of 100 hours is one-third of the starting 300 hours.

items.says: The replay does not say what rebalancing change was tested.
The increase from 60% to 75% is 15 percentage points, not 15%.
items.because: Relative to the starting rate of 60%, the increase is 25%.

items.says: The hit-rate measure is undefined.
items.because: Without the hit criterion and forecast horizon, a reader cannot interpret the rates.

items.says: The strongest project result is not the opening line.
items.because: Moving the measured before-and-after forecast result first would show the project’s clearest evidence of impact immediately.

items.says: The minutes are not clearly identified as wait time.
The line does not say how repeat visitors were matched.
items.because: A reader cannot assess the analysis without knowing the identifier or rule used to derive the household count.

items.says: The household result is not quantified and is buried in a wordy explanation.
Passive phrasing leaves the candidate’s role in cleaning the logs unclear.
The guide’s monthly use has no stated duration.
